lead.headline: Voyager 1 Switches Off Gadgets to Keep Going
lead.deck: The old space probe is now one light-day from Earth. Engineers save its power by turning things off.
body: Imagine a flashlight with a fading battery. You would switch off what you did not need. Engineers do that for Voyager 1.
On 18 November, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth, NASA says. A light-day is how far light travels in one day. That is 16.094 billion miles, NASA says.
So why turn things off? Voyager 1 makes electricity from plutonium, which slowly gives off heat. NASA says each Voyager probe loses about 4 watts of power a year.
Less power means hard choices. In April 2026, engineers shut down an instrument called LECP. The Cosmic Ray Subsystem has been off since 25 February 2025. The cameras went off in 1990.
Two science instruments still worked in April.

science.headline: Telescopes Catch a Star in the Middle of Blowing Up
science.deck: Astronomers spotted a new supernova in a faraway galaxy before it had grown its brightest.
body: Stars do not shine forever. Some end with a giant blast called a supernova. On 2 November 2026, astronomers reported a new one, SN 2026ahvu.
So who spotted it first? A system called ATLAS did. ATLAS is a set of robotic telescopes, run by computers, in both halves of Earth. It reported the blast first.

The star is in NGC 1433, a spiral galaxy. A galaxy is a huge island of stars. Space.com says NGC 1433 is about 50 million light-years away. A light-year is how far light travels in one year. So that light left the star long ago.
Next, scientists asked what kind of blast it was. They used a tool on the Keck telescope called DEIMOS. It spreads light into colours. They showed a Type Ia supernova.
The timing was lucky. Science News reports the blast had not yet reached its peak brightness. On 9 November, the Gemini South telescope in Chile took a picture of the galaxy and the new supernova.

world.kicker: AROUND THE WORLD  •  BOLIVIA AND MEXICO
world.headline: Three Countries Lose Their Measles-Free Status
world.deck: Health officials say measles now keeps spreading in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States. Vaccines hold it back.
body: Measles is an illness that spreads very easily. On 17 November, PAHO, a health group for the Americas, said three countries lost their measles-free status. They are Bolivia, Mexico and the United States.
That status is called measles elimination. A country loses it when the same measles virus spreads without a break for 12 months or more. Experts call this endemic spread.
How does a vaccine stop this? A vaccinated person is protected, so the virus has fewer people to jump to. NPR reports that about 95 percent of children need the vaccine to block its spread.

That number is where the trouble starts. NPR reports that about 92 percent of US kindergartners had the vaccine in 2025. In 2019, it was 95 percent. NPR also reports more than 5,400 US cases and 10 linked deaths.
Is measles now everywhere in the US? No, says the CDC. It says risk is highest where fewer people are vaccinated. The US can win the status back if it stops measles spreading for at least 12 months.

illustration.title: A SHIELD CALLED VACCINATION
illustration.subtitle: Bolivia, Mexico, US
illustration.caption: About 95 percent of children need the measles vaccine to block spread. About 92 percent of US kindergartners had it in 2025.

world.connect: Geography: Bolivia is in the middle of South America, while Mexico and the United States are in North America. Measles viruses do not stop at borders, which is why a group covering the whole region, PAHO, tracks them.

sports.title: SPORTS CORNER
sports.body: Sabita Toppo won the women's 100m hurdles gold at the BIMSTEC U-23 athletics meet in Bhubaneswar, India, a meet for athletes under 23. Her win helped India extend its medal lead. Hurdlers sprint and leap over barriers without slowing down. Try a cushion hurdle race at home: line up three soft cushions, then run and jump each one, keeping your rhythm steady.

challenge.title: BE VOYAGER'S ENGINEER
body: Give each player 5 coins for one day of power. List 8 gadgets in your home, such as a lamp, a radio, a fan and a toy. Each gadget costs 1 to 3 coins to run. You may spend only 5 coins, so you must switch some gadgets off.

Choose carefully. Which gadgets are the most useful? Voyager 1's engineers made the same kind of choice. They kept the plasma wave and magnetic field instruments and switched off others. Talk about why you chose what you did.
Bonus, be a supernova spotter: draw a night sky of 10 dots. Ask a friend to change one dot while you look away. Then compare the two pictures. Can you find the new star?

did_you_know.text: Light from the Moon takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach Earth. A light-year, the distance light travels in a year, is nearly 6 trillion miles. That is why even light from the nearest big galaxies takes millions of years to reach us.

explainer.title: HOW A STAR EXPLODES
body: A Type Ia supernova starts with a white dwarf. A white dwarf is the small, dense core left behind by a star like our Sun. It is no longer burning, but it is still hot. Scientists think some white dwarfs blow up after they gain extra matter, the stuff that things are made of.

From far away, scientists cannot see this happen. Instead, they use spectroscopy, which spreads starlight into a rainbow. Each material in an exploding star leaves its own marks in the rainbow. Reading them tells scientists what kind of explosion it was.
That is why catching a supernova early matters. Early light shows the first moments of a blast, which are over in just a short time.
